title: Presentation of data and observations

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Presenting a whole experiment in one table of results: drawing it up before taking readings, recording everything with consistent precision, headings that carry quantity and unit, calculated columns with justified significant figures, and then the graph - axes labelled, scales chosen to fill the grid, false origins, points plotted accurately, lines of best fit and tangents.

blocks.heading: One table for one experiment
blocks.text:
All the results of an experiment go in one table of results, one row for each value of the independent variable, so the whole data set is seen together. The table is the experiment's record: raw readings, repeats and calculated values sit side by side in it, so the trend can be read down one column and nothing needs a second sheet. A data set scattered across margins, scratch paper and memory is a data set half lost, and a table that mixes two experiments in one grid is two half-records.

The single-table rule also keeps the arithmetic honest. A calculated value written in the same row as the readings it came from can be checked against them at a glance; the same value written on a loose sheet cannot, and the check is where errors in arithmetic are caught before they become errors in conclusion.

The single table is also where the experiment becomes visible as a whole. A trend that only appears down a column - resistance rising with every length, T² growing steadily - is seen while there is still time to extend the range or add a repeat, because the whole data set is in front of the experimenter at once. Data spread across scraps shows nothing until it is assembled, and by then the apparatus is down and the chance has gone.

Rows and columns have a shape. Down the table, one row per value of the independent variable, ordered from smallest to largest. Across it, a column for every quantity that was read, then a column for each quantity calculated from them. The table drawn this way is a finished structure waiting to be filled: an experiment with a table like that has already decided what it will measure, and the readings only have to arrive.

blocks.heading: Recording everything, at the moment it is read
blocks.text:
Every reading is written into the table as it is taken, including repeats and any reading that looks unusual, because a reading not written down at the bench may be lost or wrongly remembered. The unusual reading is the important one to record: a value that seems wrong is evidence of something - a genuine fluctuation, a slipped clamp, a misread scale - and the honest table shows it, repeats it and lets the mean argue with it. Crossing it out quietly removes the experiment's only trace of what actually happened.

A reading is recorded at the moment it is taken, with its unit, so the record stays complete even if the experiment is interrupted or the apparatus is taken down. Readings taken first and written up later are copied, and copying is where numbers change: a 4 becomes a 9, a decimal point slides, a unit is added in the wrong column. The bench table is the original; anything written up afterwards is a copy of a copy.

The repeats earn their own space. Each repeat is written in its own place - separate columns for T1 and T2, or a row per repeat - and the mean is written in its own column beside them, never written over the repeats it came from. The mean that replaces its evidence is a number pretending to be exact, and the scatter it hides was the only measure of how much the readings deserved to be trusted.

Recording as you go also disciplines the hand. Numbers are written clearly the first time, in the column they belong to, because the next reading is arriving and there will not be a second chance at the first. A digit rewritten over another is a digit nobody can read later, at exactly the moment the table is being checked for the trend. The bench record written once, clearly, completely, is worth more than a fair copy written after - and it is the only one that was actually there when the apparatus was.

blocks.heading: Drawing the table before the first reading
blocks.text:
The table is drawn up before the first reading is taken, so the readings go straight into it and are not copied up later, where copying can introduce errors. The preparation is itself an act of planning: to draw the table, the experimenter has to have decided what will be read, what will be calculated from it, how many readings the range allows and where the repeats will sit. A table drawn in advance is the method written as a grid.

The size is settled the same way. The number of columns is fixed by the quantities to be recorded - each raw reading, each repeat, each calculated value - and the number of rows by the readings planned across the range. A space is ready for every reading before it exists, so no reading arrives at a table with nowhere to go, and no column is squeezed in afterwards with a heading squeezed above it.

At the bench the pay-off is speed as well as accuracy. Readings arrive every minute or two; an experimenter writing straight into a prepared table spends that interval watching the apparatus, not ruling lines. The one who draws the table first finishes earlier and holds a cleaner record than the one who "writes it up after".

blocks.heading: Raw columns and calculated columns
blocks.text:
The table carries one column for every raw reading and further columns for each quantity calculated from them, so each calculated value sits beside the readings it came from. The raw columns come first, the calculated ones after: a reader moves left to right from what was measured to what was worked out, and each value can be traced back one step.

Each calculated column is filled in the same table as the raw readings, because a value worked out away from its raw readings cannot be checked against them. The check matters more than the calculation: squaring a period, dividing a length by an area - these are a keystroke each, and the keystroke is where the error lives. A calculated column sitting beside its raw columns lets the eye run the arithmetic again, row by row, and that is what makes the table a record rather than a claim.

The split also protects the raw data itself. Raw readings are what the instruments said, and they stay as they were taken: not overwritten, not rounded again, not improved after the fact. The calculated columns carry the interpretation, and if the interpretation changes - a different quantity plotted, a different equation tested - the raw columns still hold the original readings to recalculate from. Data that survives its own analysis is data worth taking.

A column earns its place by being used. A calculated column exists because the analysis needs it - T² because the plot is of T², 1/I because the equation linearises that way - and a column calculated "because it might be useful" is work with no reader. The calculation is chosen when the table is drawn up, from the equation the experiment is testing, which is one more reason the table is drawn before the first reading: the analysis was designed then too.

blocks.heading: Headings: quantity / unit
blocks.text:
Every column heading is written as quantity / unit - L / mm, T / s, T² / s², I / mA - with the unit of a calculated column worked out from its calculation. The form is a convention, and the convention does two jobs: the reader is told what the numbers are, and told what unit they are in, before reading a single one of them.

The separator matters because the heading is read as arithmetic. T² / s² says "this column holds T squared, measured in seconds squared": the unit is squared because the quantity is, and the slash carries that reasoning. Leave out the separator - "T² s²" - and the heading says nothing a reader can parse; leave out the unit - "length" - and the column holds numbers with no meaning attached.

A calculated column's unit follows from its calculation, and the calculation is where it is checked. A column of T² calculated from T / s carries the unit s², written T² / s². A column of 1/I calculated from I / A carries the unit A⁻¹, written 1/I / A⁻¹ - odd-looking, and correct: reciprocal current, reciprocal amperes. A column of cross-section area from d² with d in mm holds mm². The test of any heading is whether a reader can tell the unit of every number in the column; a heading that fails it makes the whole column unreadable, however correct the numbers are.

blocks.heading: Consistent precision in the raw columns
blocks.text:
Raw readings of one quantity are recorded to the same number of decimal places, matching the resolution of the instrument used to take them. A rule reading to 1 mm gives lengths in whole millimetres - 245 mm, 613 mm - and every length in the column is written to the millimetre. A micrometer gives a wire's diameter to 0.01 mm, and every diameter is written to two decimal places: 0.46 mm, not 0.5 mm, and never 0.46 mm in one row and 0.5 mm in the next.

The number of decimal places in a raw reading shows the resolution of the instrument, so a change of precision inside one column misstates the instrument used. A column of lengths that runs 245, 613, 702.5 has not recorded a cleverer reading at the end; it has recorded a different instrument, or a guess, and no reader can tell which. Mixed precision in one column is the commonest presentation failure on the bench, and it costs marks every time because the inconsistency is visible at a glance.

Consistency is kept even where the reading ends in a zero. A micrometer reading exactly 0.50 mm is written 0.50 mm, not 0.5 mm: the trailing zero records the second decimal place the instrument resolved. The same holds for a digital display - what the display shows is written in full, because the display's last digit is its resolution, and dropping it drops the instrument out of its own record.

blocks.heading: Calculating in the table
blocks.text:
Calculated quantities are computed from the raw readings in the table, in the table, so the arithmetic can be checked against the readings it used. The calculation is done for one row at a time, and each row is completed before the next is begun: a table half-calculated is a table whose trend cannot yet be seen, and the trend is the reason the column exists.

A calculated quantity is worked out from the readings in its own row, so each row is complete in itself. T² in a row uses the T of that row, and nothing else; the mean of the repeats in a row uses those repeats, and no others. Row-wise work is what makes the table auditable: any value can be checked with the two or three numbers beside it, and an error found is an error found in one row, not spread through the column.

The habit also catches the physics. Calculating row by row, the experimenter watches each result appear - T² growing as L grows, R rising with each length - and a value that breaks the pattern is seen in the row where it happened. An arithmetic slip caught at row three costs a second; the same slip discovered at the graph stage costs the trend line, and discovered at the conclusion costs the experiment.

blocks.heading: Showing the working
blocks.text:
Working is shown for each calculated value: the equation in symbols, the substitution of the readings, and the result with its unit, so another reader can follow each step. The equation is named first - T = t/n, R = V/I, A = πd²/4 - because the symbols are the argument: they say what was divided by what, and why. The substitution follows, the readings put into the equation, and then the result, with its unit.

Each step of the working carries its unit, so a slip in the arithmetic or in a unit is visible where it happens. Units multiplying and cancelling along the working are the check that the physics was set up right: mm² divided by mm leaves mm, and a result labelled mm² after that division has announced its own error. A number alone is not an answer; the unit is half of it, and it is half that is lost first.

The working earns its marks as well as its honesty. A calculation marked in steps gives the equation and the substitution their own credit before the final answer, so a slip late in the working still holds the marks for the steps before it, and a marker can see exactly where a wrong answer went wrong. Working shown is working that can be marked; a bare number, right or wrong, is a claim with no visible support.

blocks.heading: Significant figures, used and justified
blocks.text:
A calculated value is given to the number of significant figures of the raw data with the fewest, or one more, and the choice is justified by naming the raw value it follows. Diameters read to 0.01 mm are given to two or three significant figures; the areas calculated from them are quoted to match, and the justification is written beside the first calculated value: "d is given to 2 significant figures, so A is given to 3" - one more, because the multiplication of π does not degrade what the measurement carried.

The significant figures of a calculated value follow the raw data, not the calculator's display, which shows every digit it can hold. A calculator told 0.462 squared will offer 0.213444, and writing that down claims a precision the 0.462 never had: the instrument resolved two decimal places, the measurement carries two, and the result pretending to six is a claim about the calculator, not about the wire. Quoting more figures than the raw data justify is the error; the test is which raw value has the fewest.

The justification is worth a mark of its own on Paper 3, and it is earned by one sentence naming the raw value with the fewest significant figures and stating what was done. The sentence is not decoration: it is the evidence that the figures in the column were chosen rather than copied, and choosing them is the skill the question is testing.

Significant figures are not the same as decimal places, and the two rules live in different columns. Raw readings keep decimal places - the instrument's resolution - and every reading in the column keeps the same number. Calculated values keep significant figures - what the raw data can support - and the number is justified against the raw values. A calculated column written "to two decimal places" has applied the raw column's rule where it does not belong: 0.585 s² and 1.131 s² carry the same three significant figures, and that is the standard the column is held to.

blocks.heading: A table worked through
blocks.text:
An experiment hangs loads on a spring and times twenty oscillations for each load, twice. The raw readings and the calculated columns for the first two rows:

| m / g | t1 / s | t2 / s | mean t / s | T / s | T² / s² |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | 15.2 | 15.4 | 15.3 | 0.765 | 0.585 |
| 200 | 14.3 | 14.5 | 14.4 | 0.720 | 0.518 |

Row one: the mean of the repeats is (15.2 + 15.4) ÷ 2 = 30.6 ÷ 2 = 15.3 s. The period is T = t ÷ 20 = 15.3 ÷ 20 = 0.765 s. The square is T² = 0.765 × 0.765 = 0.585225 s², written 0.585 s² to three significant figures: the raw times carry three, so the calculated column carries three, justified by naming t1 and t2 as the raw values with the fewest.

Row two: the mean is (14.3 + 14.5) ÷ 2 = 28.8 ÷ 2 = 14.4 s, the period is 14.4 ÷ 20 = 0.720 s, and T² = 0.720 × 0.720 = 0.5184 s², written 0.518 s². Every raw column keeps the precision its instrument set - the masses in whole grams, the times to 0.1 s - and every calculated column keeps the significant figures its raw data justify. Six rows later the table holds one experiment, complete, checkable row by row.

blocks.heading: Labelling the graph axes
blocks.text:
Each graph axis is labelled with the quantity and its unit, written quantity / unit - the same convention as a table heading. The x-axis carries the independent variable, L / m; the y-axis carries whatever was calculated to plot against it, T² / s². The axis is the table column it came from, drawn rather than listed, and it is labelled the same way so a reader moves between table and graph without converting.

The unit on the axis is what makes a gradient meaningful later. A gradient read from "T² / s² against L / m" is in s² m⁻¹ before it is even calculated - the units of the axes fix the unit of the gradient - and an axis labelled "length" and "time squared" gives a gradient that belongs to no quantity at all. The label is written along the axis, close under it or beside it, in the same quantity / unit form as the column heading.

The label also fixes which variable is which. The independent variable goes on the x-axis, the calculated dependent value on the y-axis, and the graph is described in that order: T² against L, R against 1/A. A graph drawn the other way round is not a wrong answer, it is a different experiment, and every gradient and intercept read from it answers a question nobody asked.

One graph answers one question. When the analysis needs a second plot - R against 1/A as well as R against L - it is drawn as its own graph with its own axes, not squeezed onto the first grid with a second pair of labels. Two trends on one grid is neither trend drawn well, and each gradient read from it is half of a measurement.

blocks.heading: Choosing scales that fill the grid
blocks.text:
Scales are chosen so the plotted points cover at least half of the graph grid in both the x- and the y-direction, which usually means starting each axis just below the smallest reading. The grid is a fixed area of squares; the readings are a fixed set of values; the scale is the meeting of the two, and a good one spends the grid on the data instead of on empty space.

Where the smallest reading lies far from zero, the grid is filled by starting the axis near that smallest reading, and that choice is what makes at least half of the grid usable. Lengths running 0.700 m to 1.200 m plotted from zero spend more than half the x-axis on the range 0 to 0.700, where no readings sit; started at 0.600, the same readings stretch across the whole grid. The axis that starts away from zero is a false origin, and it is the standard instrument for data that does not begin at zero.

Scales are chosen as 1, 2 or 5 units to a 2 cm square, times a power of ten, so each small square is a simple fraction of the unit and values read off easily. An awkward scale, such as 3 or 7 units to a square, turns every reading into a mental division, which is where reading errors begin - a point at 0.945 m is plain on a 0.05-per-square scale and a puzzle on a 0.03-per-square one. The test of a scale is whether the points spread over at least half the grid each way, and whether each 2 cm square stands for 1, 2 or 5 units times a power of ten.

blocks.heading: False origins
blocks.text:
A false origin is used where the readings begin a long way from zero: the axis starts at a convenient value just below the smallest reading instead of at zero. It is the scale choice carried one step further - the axis begins where the data begins - and it is used wherever a zero start would compress the points into a corner of the grid.

A false origin is marked on the axis with its value, and the labels count up from it, so a reader can see that the axis does not start at zero. The starting value is written on the axis in the ordinary way, as the first label; nothing else changes, except that the x-axis no longer shows x = 0. An unlabelled break is not a false origin, it is a trap: a reader who cannot see where the axis starts cannot read anything off the graph safely.

The false origin buys a full grid for the data, and it costs one habit in return: the y-intercept can no longer be read off the graph, because the y-axis the graph shows is not the y-axis at x = 0. Where a false origin is used and an intercept is needed, the intercept is calculated from c = y − mx with a point on the line - the calculation is carried in this topic's third section, and the rule belongs there; the warning belongs here, at the moment the axis is drawn.

Whether to use one is a judgement the data settle. Lengths from 0.700 m to 1.200 m plotted from zero fill barely half the grid, and the lost half is where the accuracy of the gradient lived; the same readings on an axis started at 0.600 m stretch across the full grid. But readings that begin near zero - masses from 100 g up, say - are plotted from zero, where the axis is honest, the intercept is readable and the grid is already full. The false origin is a tool for data far from zero, not a habit for every graph.

blocks.heading: Labelling along the axes
blocks.text:
Numerical labels are written at regular intervals along the whole of each axis, at least every 2 cm, so any plotted point can be read against a labelled line. The labels are the graph's addressing scheme: a reader finding a gradient needs two labelled points on the line, a reader checking a plot needs to find a reading's coordinate, and both navigate by the labels alone.

Labels are spaced at a constant interval, because a stretch of unlabelled squares forces a reader to count them, and counting is where mistakes enter. The interval is chosen with the scale - 0.2 per label, 0.5 per label, whatever the 1-2-5 scale of the axis makes natural - and it is kept the whole length of the axis. The last label sits at or just beyond the largest reading, not short of it: an axis labelled to 1.0 when the readings run to 1.200 has left its final 2 cm anonymous.

The labels are the numbers of the scale, written small and clear, with the unit already named in the axis label so the numbers themselves stay bare. The discipline is small and the effect is not: a fully labelled axis is what makes a graph a measuring instrument rather than a sketch.

The two axes are labelled to the same standard, including the one that was easiest to forget. An x-axis labelled every 2 cm and a y-axis labelled at its start and finish is half an instrument: the gradient's Δy is read from the y-axis, and an unlabelled y-axis turns every gradient into an estimate. Both axes, whole length, constant interval - that is the whole rule.

blocks.heading: Plotting the points
blocks.text:
Points are plotted as small, accurate crosses placed to better than 1 mm, and each is checked against its coordinates before the line is drawn. A cross is used because it is honest: two thin strokes, one on each coordinate, and the reading sits where they cross. The check matters because plotting is transcription, and transcription is where a correct table becomes a wrong graph - the x-reading placed against the y-column is the classic slip.

A point plotted as a large dot covers the small squares around it, so its position is uncertain by the width of the dot. A dot 2 mm across on a scale of 0.05 m per square has swallowed 0.05 m of the x-axis; a cross of fine 1 mm strokes holds the reading to the square it was meant for. The same argument bans the felt-tip and rewards the sharp pencil: a plotted point is a measurement, and a measurement is only as good as its smallest marking.

Accuracy of plotting is checked by re-reading: after the last point is down, the eye runs the plotted points against the table once more, matching each cross to its row. A point off the trend by a full square is re-plotted before it is suspected of being bad data - most often it is a transcription slip, and the table catches it. Only a point that is plotted right and still sits off the trend is evidence about the physics.

blocks.heading: The line of best fit
blocks.text:
The line of best fit is a single straight line or smooth curve with the points balanced on either side of it along its whole length; it is not drawn through the first and last points alone. The line is the experimenter's statement of the trend, and the trend is the whole point of the graph: the line says what the data, taken together, show.

A straight line of best fit leaves roughly as many points above as below, and the balance is checked along the whole line, not at one end of it. The checking is what "best" means: a line through the first and last points ignores every reading between them, a line through the origin answers a question the data were not asked, and a line bent to touch a favourite point is a line the data do not support. The honest line lets the scatter fall where it falls, evenly either side.

Where the trend is curved, the curve is drawn as a single smooth line through the points, again balanced - a smooth curve, not a join of straight segments between points, because the trend is the physics and the physics does not turn corners at every reading. The curve is drawn in one sweep, and its smoothness is checked by the same standard: points alternating above and below as it passes.

The line serves two masters and serves both honestly. For the gradient, the line is the thing measured: two points on the line, far apart, give Δy and Δx, and nothing in the table matters once the line is drawn - which is why the line deserves the same care as a reading. For the conclusion, the line is the evidence: the scatter of the points about it shows how far the data can be trusted, and a line drawn to flatter one point has quietly re-run the experiment with one reading. The line drawn with a transparent ruler, in one movement, balanced either side - that is the whole skill.

blocks.heading: Tangents to a curve
blocks.text:
A tangent to a curve at a point is a straight line drawn to touch the curve at that point, with the same slope as the curve there; its gradient is found from two widely separated points on the tangent. The tangent is how a curve is measured: a curve's gradient at a point is the gradient of the tangent there, and it changes along the curve, so a fresh tangent is drawn at each point where a rate is needed.

Drawing one is a physical skill with a physical trick. The tangent is drawn with a ruler laid on the curve at the point, adjusted until the line touches the curve at that point only - resting on it, not cutting through. A common aid: mirror the ruler's angle by rolling the ruler in tiny steps and watch the contact; the tangent is the position where the ruler rests on the point without crossing the curve on either side of it.

The tangent is measured like any line. Two points on the tangent itself, far apart, are read, and the gradient between them is the curve's gradient at the point of contact - a rate at an instant, in the unit of y divided by the unit of x. A tangent drawn short and steep is a guess; a tangent drawn long enough to span half the grid is a measurement.

Tangents appear in this course wherever a rate changes. A distance-time curve steepens as a trolley runs away downhill, and the speed at an instant is the gradient of the tangent drawn there; a cooling curve flattens as the temperature falls, and the rate of cooling at an instant is read the same way. Each tangent is drawn at a stated point, named with its x-value, because a gradient "somewhere on the curve" is not a measurement of anywhere in particular.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: Presentation turns the measurement skills of 12.1 into data a graph can carry, and it hands the analysis of 12.3 everything it reads. Topic 1's significant figures and unit conventions are the rules the headings follow; topics 7 and 8 use these graphing skills on waves and interference patterns; topics 9 and 10 fill these tables with electrical readings; topic 6's Hooke's law experiment is drawn and plotted exactly this way. The table drawn up in advance and the graph scaled to fill the grid are the same craft wherever the physics comes from.
